summary: This benchmark evaluates whether fine-tuning the complete final transformer block (attention plus MLP) of Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B improves performance and transferability over tuning the feed-forward module alone on a Python repair task. Through a rigorous 2x2 factorial ablation and paired bootstrap confidence intervals, the authors convincingly demonstrate a negative result: unfreezing attention yields a negligible +0.13 point gain, fails pre-registered transfer gates against the Qwen2.5-1.5B host, and is outperformed by a trivial output-counting heuristic.
strengths: Rigorous statistical methodology employing pre-registered gating criteria, multi-seed training, and 5,000 paired family-bootstrap resamples.
Comprehensive factorial ablation isolating the contributions of self-attention, layer normalizations, and feed-forward modules.
Thorough error and artifact analysis revealing that an arithmetic shortcut on assertion outputs solves 81.84% of tasks without parsing code structure.
Transparent reporting of negative results and inclusion of logit-level replay checks demonstrating numerical consistency.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies on a highly synthetic indentation-repair benchmark rather than realistic, multi-token software engineering datasets (e.g., SWE-bench or HumanEval).
Small sample size of 16 families across 512 qualification and confirmation repairs limits statistical power for fine-grained interaction effects.
No formal supporting repository was submitted directly through the platform submission system, relying instead on external repository links.
suggestions: Evaluate whether similar component-restoration and attention-adaptation behaviors hold across earlier transformer layers or across more diverse, natural programming benchmarks.
Filter or modify the synthetic benchmark generator to eliminate the identified bonus-output arithmetic shortcut so that models cannot exploit trivial frequency cues.
Formally bundle benchmark code and evaluation harness data into the submission platform package for turnkey archival reproducibility.

claims.text: The adapted donor block has 14,912,384 parameters, including 13,074,432 feed-forward weights.

A preceding study trained only the final feed-forward module of Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, while the native Qwen2.5-1.5B control could adapt its entire final block. That asymmetry left open whether giving the donor the same access to attention would create a useful expert. [Revisiting Model Stitching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07682)

novelty_vs_existing.title: Revisiting Model Stitching to Compare Neural Representations
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Applies layer/component stitching specifically to fine-grained transformer sub-modules (attention vs. FFN in the final block) in modern open-weights code LLMs rather than standard layer-boundary stitching.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Qwen2.5-Coder Technical Report
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Uses Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B and 1.5B architectures as donor and host subjects to audit modular transferability and failure modes of selective block adaptation.
